title: On Curiosity — Sharif Shameem, Lexica

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on programming models through prompts, few-shot examples, parallel prompt orchestration, and compiler-style LLM programming to discover latent capabilities. The talk is cross-domain AI engineering philosophy grounded in personal computing visions from Licklider and individual exploration through demos. The talk focuses on curiosity-driven ideation and demo-based prototyping rather than production deployment or maintenance. Following the technical demos and historical capability progression requires familiarity with AI models, context windows, and software development. Recorded conference talk at the AI Engineer World's Fair featuring live demo walkthroughs, historical narrative, and audience Q&A. summary:
Shameem delivers a talk on curiosity and demos as essential tools for AI engineering. His central argument is that curiosity—the subconscious recognition of patterns surfacing as a feeling—is the main force for pulling ideas from the future into the present. He traces this through Poincaré's account of unconscious mathematical discovery on a bus and frames demos as the best expression of curiosity to the world.

He walks through several demos spanning 2020 to 2025. In 2020, working with GPT-3's 2,000-token context window at $75 per million output tokens, he built a browser-based JSX compiler inspired by Bret Victor's immediate feedback principle. A banking app demo from the same era—where bugs let users zero out debt by giving money away—he describes as the start of vibe coding. Another demo required three parallel prompts joined in the background to generate full applications within tiny context limits. A 'Multivac' demo broke ambitious problems like climate change into sub-problems for the model to reason through visually. In 2021, with context expanded to roughly 4,000 tokens, he tested model agency by having GPT-3 attempt to buy AirPods in a browser, requiring a custom HTML parser to compress 24,000-token web pages. A recent demo by his friend Farsza uses Gemini 2.5 Pro for video-first basketball coaching with a Michael Jordan feedback persona; an audience member reports applying it to running and getting feedback comparable to a $600/month coach.

Shameem argues AI engineering differs fundamentally from traditional engineering. Citing Hamming—'if you know what you're doing, you should not be doing it'—he frames AI engineering as excavation: searching for hidden capabilities with curiosity as a flashlight. He notes even OpenAI researchers didn't know GPT-3 could browse the web or generate React components. He compares exploring model capabilities to crossing a foggy pond stone by stone. He references a tweet comparing Claude to an intergalactic spaceship sold as a toaster. He describes his mental model of AI as intelligent beings you hook up to apparatuses, instilling tools with purpose and agency. His motivation stems from frustration that powerful models' capabilities remain unexplored and a moral obligation to computing pioneers like Licklider and Alan Kay, whose 1960s visions—such as an assistant with perfect context—remain unrealized while we rebuild the same applications. He closes with Licklider's 'Man-Computer Symbiosis,' arguing we have a moral obligation to explore and share what these tools can do.

Demos are the best way to explore and express what's possible with AI models—you learn by interacting, not by theorizing

sections.title: Introduction and the Curiosity Argument
sections.summary: Shameem introduces himself as founder of Lexica and states his main argument: curiosity is the main force for pulling ideas from the future into the present. He cites Poincaré's account of unconscious mathematical discovery while boarding a bus, where weeks of stuck work suddenly resolved, and Poincaré declared the role of unconscious work in invention as incontestable.

sections.title: The Pattern of Demo Creation
sections.summary: Shameem describes the recurring pattern of his demos: starting with a great idea, realizing it seems impossible, pushing through with sheer determination despite tiny context windows, and feeling pride upon success. He argues the most important thing about good demos is exploring what's possible with models by interacting with them, and the way to make interesting demos is by following curiosity.

sections.title: 2020 GPT-3 Demos
sections.summary: Shameem shows 2020 demos built with GPT-3's 2,000-token context window at $75 per million output tokens. A JSX compiler in the browser, inspired by Bret Victor's immediate feedback principle, felt magical. An interactive demo required three parallel prompts joined in the background to generate full applications within tiny context limits. He notes today's Claude system prompt alone is 25,000 tokens.

sections.title: 2021 Agency Demo
sections.summary: With context expanded to ~4,000 tokens in 2021, Shameem tested whether models had agency by tasking GPT-3 with buying AirPods in Chrome. Web pages like Walmart.com were 24,000 tokens, so he built a custom HTML parser to compress them. The demo failed spectacularly—getting distracted by terms of service—but revealed that models pre-trained on web text had internal agency in their weights, which we now take for granted.

sections.title: Gemini 2.5 Pro Demo and Low-Hanging Fruit
sections.summary: Shameem shows a recent demo by his friend Farsza using Gemini 2.5 Pro: a basketball shot tracker that provides feedback as Michael Jordan watching gameplay. He argues this reveals video-first experiences are now possible. He claims that if you froze all model capabilities today—no new training—you could still build amazing products for the next 10 years by exploring existing latent capabilities through demos.

sections.title: AI Engineering as Excavation
sections.summary: Citing Richard Hamming—'if you know what you're doing, you should not be doing it'—Shameem distinguishes AI engineering from traditional goal-oriented engineering. AI engineering is closer to excavating: searching for hidden capabilities with curiosity as a flashlight. He notes even OpenAI and Anthropic researchers don't fully understand their models' capabilities, with OpenAI researchers unaware GPT-3 could browse the web or generate React components.

sections.title: Darwin, the Foggy Pond, and Uncertainty
sections.summary: Shameem recounts Darwin spending eight years studying barnacles—thought crazy by others—before publishing evolution, showing work and play are indistinguishable in the moment. He compares exploring model capabilities to crossing a foggy pond: stepping stone by stone, unable to plan the route ahead. He cites a tweet comparing Claude to an intergalactic spaceship sold as a toaster, emphasizing latent capabilities we overlook. Uncertainty is at the core of AI engineering.

sections.title: Moral Obligation and Closing
sections.summary: Shameem closes with Licklider's 1960s paper 'Man-Computer Symbiosis,' noting vacuum tube computers and punch cards were state of the art then. He argues Licklider would have done anything for an hour with today's tools, and that we have a moral obligation to those who came before us to follow our curiosity and share what we explore with the world.

sections.title: Q&A: Running Coach Application
sections.summary: An audience member reports applying the basketball demo to running, getting feedback comparable to a $600/month running coach—including per-step gait analysis that a human coach could never provide. Shameem then begins pulling additional archived demos.

sections.title: Q&A: 2020 Banking App and Vibe Coding
sections.summary: Shameem shows a 2020 GPT-3 banking app demo built weeks after the API launched, with a browser-based compiler for visual back-and-forth. Bugs were humorous—giving away money while in debt zeroed the balance. He calls this the start of vibe coding and describes his mental model of AI as intelligent beings hooked up to apparatuses with instilled purpose and agency. He discovered GPT-3 after someone told him OpenAI had created AGI.

sections.title: Q&A: Base Models and Motivation
sections.summary: Confirming GPT-3 was a base model with no instruct version until about a year later, Shameem explains prompting relied on few-shot examples. He then discusses his motivation: frustration that powerful models' capabilities go unexplored, and a moral obligation to computing pioneers like Licklider and Alan Kay, whose 1960s visions—such as an assistant with perfect context—remain unrealized while we rebuild the same applications. He contrasts Licklider's vision with ChatGPT's amnesia across new chats.

sections.title: Q&A: Multivac Demo
sections.summary: Shameem shows Multivac, a GPT-3 demo for solving ambitious problems by breaking them into visual sub-problems—e.g., climate change decomposed into vegetarianism, wind turbines, and solar panels. He argues models are reasoning assistants for big problems, not just text completers, and could one day generate ideas autonomously as thought partners. He suggests someone rebuild it with current models like Opus Max.
